title: The Only Fever in the World
subtitle: Krishna spares the defeated Jvara and grants him dominion over fever
story:
The great battle of Sonitpura had stopped. An invisible voice had spoken out of the sky, and god and demon alike on that field had gone still.

It was a war that had drawn the gods themselves in: Krishna had come against Vana, the thousand-armed king who served Shiva, and Shiva had sent his own creatures to fight for Vana. One of them was Jvara, the fever. Earlier, the burning demon had slipped inside Krishna's body — for a while Krishna's steps had grown heavy, his hair had stood on end, he had yawned and sighed without cease and steadied himself with one hand on the ground, until at last he shook the weakness off. He had drawn the demon out by creating from his own strength a second fever, more dreadful than the first, which had seized Jvara and dragged him from Krishna's body. Now the creature lay pinned under Krishna's hand, and Krishna, angry, had thrown him to the earth and was about to tear him apart — when the voice spoke: "Do not kill this Jvara. He is worthy of being protected by you."

Krishna heard, and let the fever go. Jvara rose and prostrated himself at Krishna's feet. "Grant me this one boon," he said. "Let me be the only fever in this world, and let no other flourish beside me."

"It is proper to grant a boon to one who asks for it," Krishna said, "and you have asked for my protection. Go in peace, Jvara. You will have what you pray for. As before, you will be the only fever — and may the one I created dissolve in me."

And the counter-fever Krishna had made melted back into his own being, as frost melts into the morning.

Then Krishna told the fever how it would live from that day on. "Divide yourself into three parts. With one, enter the four-legged animals; with the second, the trees and stones and all things that do not move; with the third, human beings. And of that third part, take a fourth portion, and let it live always among the birds." So among people the fever would come in four forms — returning every day, after two days, after three days, and after four. In trees it would live as the blight that pales the leaves, in fruit as blight, in lotuses as frost, in the earth as drought, in water as the weed that chokes it, in peacocks as the growing crest, in mountains as mineral, in cattle as sickness. "By your very sight and touch," Krishna said, "animals will lose their lives. Only gods and men will be able to withstand you."

Jvara was delighted. He folded his hands and saluted Krishna. "I am blessed that you give me rule over all creatures and things. I was made long ago by Shiva himself; now, vanquished by you in battle, I am your servant. Command me, and I will obey."

"Then hear the wish I cherish," Krishna said. "Any man who greets me with respect and reads this account of the great battle with full attention will be freed from fever."

"So be it," said Jvara. He saluted Krishna and left the battlefield — carrying with him, in the very shape of his existence, the mercy that had spared him.
reflection: Jvara asks not for safety but for supremacy — he wants to remain the only fever in the world — and Krishna grants the wish while redrawing its limits: the fever may range everywhere, but it returns in measured forms, and the telling of its defeat is promised to free men from it. Mercy, here, is not the erasure of an enemy but the reshaping of his power.
next_story_tease: But the fever was only one of Vana's defenders — Shiva himself was already riding toward the battlefield.
hero_scene: On the Sonitpura battlefield the defeated Jvara, a gaunt burning figure, prostrates with bent head at Krishna's feet while Krishna, radiant, raises a hand in blessing and the counter-fever he created dissolves into mist behind him.
